Moville
moh-VIL
n. (the Down monastery of Finnian, whose copied psalter provoked the quarrel that sent Columba to Iona)
Irish Magh Bhile, the plain of the sacred tree, from magh, a plain, and bile, an ancient tree.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Moville on Strangford Lough in County Down was founded about 540 by Finnian, called Finnian of Moville to distinguish him from Finnian of Clonard, a man who had studied at Whithorn and who is said to have brought a copy of the Latin Gospels back from Rome. The story attached to that book is the most famous quarrel in Irish church history: Columba copied it without permission, Finnian claimed the copy, the high king Diarmait judged for Finnian, and the dispute fed into the battle of Cúl Dreimhne in 561 in which thousands died. Columba was arraigned before a synod, and whether as sentence or as self-imposed penance he left Ireland for Iona, undertaking to win more souls than had fallen in the battle. The copy, called the Cathach, survives as the oldest Irish manuscript. The dictionary records Moville for what the episode cost and for how it ended. The sacrifices God accepts are named plainly as a broken spirit and a contrite heart, and the one place he promises to dwell besides the high and holy place is with the man who has them.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines contrite as broken-hearted for sin; a sacrifice as an offering made to God; humble as having a low opinion of oneself; to revive as to restore life or vigor; and justly as according to right.

expand to see more

CONTRITE, a. Literally, worn or bruised; hence, broken-hearted for sin; deeply affected with grief and sorrow for having offended God.

SACRIFICE, n. An offering made to God; any thing consecrated and offered to God; destruction or surrender of any thing for the sake of something else.

HUMBLE, a. Low; opposed to high or lofty; modest; meek; submissive; having a low opinion of one's self.

REVIVE, v.t. To bring again to life; to reanimate; to raise from languor or depression; to recover.

JUSTLY, adv. In a just manner; equitably; according to right; honestly; properly.

Key Scripture

Psa 51:17 — "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise."

Isa 57:15 — "For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy; I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones."

Mic 6:8 — "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?"

Joh 17:21 — "That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me."

Modern Corruption

Down monastery of Finnian of Moville, whose psalter Columba copied without leave, provoking the judgment and the battle that sent Columba to Iona.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the end of the story rather than the quarrel in it. Whatever the rights of the copied book, what came out of Cúl Dreimhne was a man undone by his own share in the slaughter, and the offering such a man can make is named exactly: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” (Psa 51:17). Isaiah adds the astonishing promise attached to that condition, that the high and lofty One dwells “with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit” (Isa 57:15).

The live temptation is to let a dispute over property, even church property, become a war, and the Irish church did exactly that over a psalter. Micah had already reduced the whole requirement to three clauses that would have prevented it: what the LORD requires is “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8). And Christ's prayer makes the unity of his people a matter of the world's belief, “That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee” (Joh 17:21). Two abbots at law over a book is the opposite of that witness; Iona was the restitution.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew dakah (H1794), broken or crushed; Hebrew dakka (H1793), contrite; Hebrew tsana (H6800), to be humble; Greek heis (G1520), one.

expand to see more

Hebrew shabar (H7665) — to break, to shatter; “a broken and a contrite heart”, Psalm 51:17.

Hebrew dakka (H1793) — crushed, contrite; “of a contrite and humble spirit”, Isaiah 57:15.

Hebrew chayah (H2421) — to live, to revive; “to revive the spirit of the humble”, Isaiah 57:15.

Hebrew chesed (H2617) — mercy, steadfast love; “and to love mercy”, Micah 6:8.

Greek heis (G1520) — one; “That they all may be one”, John 17:21.

Usage

"“The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit” (Psa 51:17) — what Columba had left to offer."

"“to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8) — what would have prevented the battle."

"“That they all may be one” (Joh 17:21) — the witness two abbots at law destroyed."
